items.title: QuPRS
items.text:
QuPRS checks equivalence of quantum circuits using Path-sum reduction and weighted model counting (WMC).

The project provides a Python interface for Qiskit circuits, a native Rust verification library, and a separately built Rust command-line program.

  • Getting started explains installation and supported environments.
  • Executable examples provide small runnable equivalence, inequality, global-phase, solver, and Rust CLI cases.
  • Verification introduces the available verification methods and result semantics.
  • Path-sum theory and weighted model counting explain the algorithms and numerical evidence.
  • API Reference links the generated Python and Rust documentation.
  • Architecture describes the relationship between the Python and native Rust interfaces.

Source code, releases, and contribution instructions are available in the QuPRS repository.

items.title: Python and Rust architecture
items.text: QuPRS provides two execution interfaces built around Path-sum reduction and weighted model counting.

items.title: Python integration
items.text:
The Python entry point QuPRS.check_equivalence() accepts supported Qiskit QuantumCircuit objects and QASM inputs. The backend argument selects either the Python implementation or the Rust implementation exposed through PyO3.

With backend="rust" and safe_mode=False (the default), Python calls the Rust extension in-process. With backend="rust" and safe_mode=True, Python instead supervises an isolated worker that loads the same PyO3 extension. Isolation bounds worker communication and enforces a worker deadline, but parent-side Qiskit serialization is not forcibly preemptible. Memory enforcement depends on operating-system support.

For backend="python", safe_mode=True uses the Python strategy's isolation mechanism; it does not run the standalone Rust CLI.

items.title: Native Rust
items.text: The pathsum crate exposes a typed verification engine and public types for native callers. Its API is documented in the Rust crate reference. The separate Rust CLI provides command-line input and process execution.

items.title: Verification paths
items.text:
• Reduction rules: try to establish a verdict by simplifying Path-sum expressions.
  • Weighted model counting: use an explicitly selected solver to classify a weighted count.
  • Hybrid: pass the residual Path-sum to WMC if reduction is inconclusive.

GPMC and Ganak are independent solver choices; solver failures do not silently imply equivalence or inequivalence. WMC numerical verdicts must be interpreted separately from exact source semantics and certified accuracy.

See the Python API for parameters and return types, and Verification for result classifications.

items.title: Executable examples
items.text:
These complete examples use the public interfaces. Each Python block is run independently by the documentation examples check using the current source build, and the shell block is checked against the native CLI. Start with installation.

All examples use one qubit so that their expected classifications are easy to audit. A timeout, solver error or unknown status is not equivalent to a successful inequality result.

items.title: 1. Exact-equivalence control (reduction rules)
items.text:
Two Hadamard gates cancel. This comparison needs no external model counter.

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from QuPRS import check_equivalence

original = QuantumCircuit(1)
optimized = QuantumCircuit(1)
optimized.h(0)
optimized.h(0)

result = check_equivalence(original, optimized, method="reduction_rules",
                           backend="python", timeout=30)
assert result.equivalent == "equivalent", result.equivalent
assert result.wmc_solver_invoked is False

items.title: 2. Inequivalent control (reduction rules)
items.text:
An X gate changes the basis-state mapping relative to the identity. This is not a global phase.

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from QuPRS import check_equivalence

original = QuantumCircuit(1)
different = QuantumCircuit(1)
different.x(0)

result = check_equivalence(original, different, method="reduction_rules",
                           backend="python", timeout=30)
assert result.equivalent == "not_equivalent", result.equivalent

items.title: 3. Global phase is a separate classification
items.text:
A scalar phase changes the operator but not its action on measurement probabilities. equivalent* is distinct from exact equivalent.

from math import pi
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from QuPRS import check_equivalence

original = QuantumCircuit(1)
phase_shifted = QuantumCircuit(1)
phase_shifted.global_phase = pi / 2

result = check_equivalence(original, phase_shifted, method="reduction_rules",
                           backend="python", timeout=30)
assert result.equivalent == "equivalent*", result.equivalent

items.title: 4. WMC-only and explicit solver selection
items.text:
The gates below differ by a nontrivial relative phase. The projective distance between I and RZ(0.2) is |sin(0.1)|, much larger than the default numerical tolerance.

Each selected solver is called explicitly; the program does not silently fall back from one to the other.

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from QuPRS import check_equivalence

original = QuantumCircuit(1)
different = QuantumCircuit(1)
different.rz(0.2, 0)

for solver in ("gpmc", "ganak"):
    result = check_equivalence(
        original, different,
        method="wmc_only", backend="python", tool_name=solver,
        approximate_distance_tolerance=1e-8, timeout=30,
    )
    assert result.equivalent == "not_equivalent", (solver, result.equivalent)
    assert result.wmc_solver_invoked is True, solver
    assert result.wmc_numerical_verdict is not None, solver

A WMC verdict is a finite-precision observation rather than a certificate of source-exact equivalence. Inspect wmc_solver_invoked and wmc_numerical_verdict separately; a reached WMC stage may still use an analytic shortcut instead of spawning a solver.

items.title: 5. Python interface to the isolated Rust backend
items.text:
backend="rust" calls the Rust engine through PyO3. Enabling safe_mode executes that extension in a supervised child process, not through the standalone Rust CLI. Isolation does not make parent-side circuit serialization preemptible and is not a universal memory guarantee.

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from QuPRS import check_equivalence

original = QuantumCircuit(1)
optimized = QuantumCircuit(1)
optimized.x(0)
optimized.x(0)

result = check_equivalence(original, optimized, method="reduction_rules",
                           backend="rust", safe_mode=True, timeout=30)
assert result.equivalent == "equivalent", result.equivalent

items.title: 6. Standalone Rust CLI
items.text:
For a source checkout with native dependencies installed, run the Rust CLI using QASM2 files. Its command-line options are not Python API arguments, and installing the Python wheel does not install a standalone CLI command.

set -eu
scratch="$(mktemp -d)"
trap 'rm -rf "$scratch"' EXIT
cat > "$scratch/identity.qasm" <<'QASM'
OPENQASM 2.0;
include "qelib1.inc";
qreg q[1];
QASM
cat > "$scratch/two-h.qasm" <<'QASM'
OPENQASM 2.0;
include "qelib1.inc";
qreg q[1];
h q[0];
h q[0];
QASM
status="$(cargo run --quiet --locked --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml -p QuPRS_cli -- \
  "$scratch/identity.qasm" "$scratch/two-h.qasm" --method reduction-rules --quiet)"
test "$status" = "equivalent"

For other supported inputs and options, see the Python API, verification methods, solver contract and architecture. Results may be unknown or resource-limited; callers must handle those states explicitly rather than treating them as not_equivalent.

items.title: Install the Python package
items.text:
QuPRS supports Python 3.11, 3.12, and 3.13 with Qiskit 1.x and 2.x. Published wheels support Linux x86-64 and ARM64, and macOS 15 or later on Intel and Apple Silicon. Windows users should use a supported Linux environment such as WSL2.

Create a virtual environment and install the package:

python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install QuPRS

For macOS and Linux, see the repository installation guide for platform-specific requirements.

items.title: Verify two circuits
items.text:
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from QuPRS import check_equivalence

original = QuantumCircuit(1)
optimized = QuantumCircuit(1)

result = check_equivalence(original, optimized, method="hybrid")
print(result.equivalent)

See the fully tested examples for positive/negative controls, global phase, GPMC/Ganak selection, isolated Rust verification, and native CLI input.

items.title: Rust users
items.text: The native Rust crate and command-line tool are maintained in the Rust workspace. The Python wheel does not install a standalone Rust CLI executable. See the CLI example for a self-contained native source-checkout invocation.

items.title: Representation
items.text:
A Path-sum represents the action of a quantum circuit on a computational-basis state as a finite sum of amplitudes indexed by Boolean path variables:

\[ U|x\rangle = \alpha\!\!\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}^{m}} e^{2\pi i P(x,y)}\,|f(x,y)\rangle. \]

Here, \(x\) is the input bit string, \(y\) is the path-variable string, \(P\) is a real-valued phase polynomial measured in cycles (one cycle is \(2\pi\) radians), \(f\) gives the output bit string, and \(\alpha\) accounts for normalization. The exact representation and allowed coefficient domains depend on the constructed PathSum; not every circuit is a sum with unit coefficients.

For a comparison, QuPRS builds an expression reflecting the input and output circuit composition. The reduction engine rewrites the Path-sum while attempting to preserve the represented operation.

items.title: Exact algebraic identities underlying the rules
items.text:
These identities hold for Boolean variables. They are algebraic checks on the rule families, not a claim that any approximate coefficient match is exact.

Elim. If an internal path variable \(y\) occurs in neither the phase \(P\) nor the output \(f\), then the two contributions are identical:

\[ \sum_{y\in\{0,1\}} e^{2\pi iP}\,|f\rangle =2e^{2\pi iP}\,|f\rangle. \]

Removing \(y\) must also preserve the total amplitude, including the path-count normalization. QuPRS finds a reducible variable only after checking that it is absent from the output and the phase.

HH. Suppose \(y_0\) does not occur in the remaining phase, output, or \(Q\), and \(y_1\) does not occur in \(Q\). Then:

\[ \sum_{y_0\in\{0,1\}} e^{2\pi i\frac12 y_0(y_1+Q)} =2\,\delta_{y_1,\,Q\bmod2}. \]

The eliminated \(y_0\) imposes a Boolean constraint; the remaining phase and output must consistently substitute \(y_1\leftarrow Q\bmod2\). In the native implementation, each phase monomial involving \(y_0\) must have the required half-cycle coefficient, and the selected singleton target must not occur elsewhere in its replacement polynomial.

Omega. If an internal \(y\) is absent from the remaining phase/output and \(Q\) is Boolean-valued, the quarter-cycle identities are:

\[ \sum_{y=0}^1e^{2\pi i\,y(\frac14+\frac12Q)} =\sqrt2\,e^{2\pi i(\frac18-\frac14Q)}, \] \[ \sum_{y=0}^1e^{2\pi i\,y(\frac34+\frac12Q)} =\sqrt2\,e^{2\pi i(-\frac18+\frac14Q)}. \]

These assume the specified quarter-cycle singleton and half-cycle cross terms; the \(\sqrt2\) amplitude factor is accounted for by the path-count normalization. They cannot be applied to an arbitrary phase coefficient.

For implementation-level applicability, see Python matching and substitutions and native Rust reduction matching. The algebraic identities appear in the TACAS 2026 QuPRS paper and earlier path-sum verification calculus.

items.title: Reduction rules
items.text:
QuPRS implements the Elim, HH, and omega families of simplifications:

Rule family Purpose Essential applicability condition Elim Remove a redundant path variable Its phase/output dependence must meet the rule's cancellation conditions HH Eliminate or constrain variables through Hadamard-related phase structure The required phase-polynomial and Boolean dependencies must match Omega Simplify a constrained root-of-unity phase sum Coefficients and variable occurrence must match the supported root-of-unity identity

These descriptions are the rule roles, not substitutes for their algebraic side conditions. An arbitrary phase polynomial or path variable cannot be eliminated just because it resembles a pattern. See the public Rust reduction implementation and Python PathSum implementation for the exact supported cases.

items.title: Exact source expressions versus approximate reduction
items.text:
The per-call rr_tolerance controls numerical coefficient matching and approximate reduction in the supported implementations. The default is 1e-10. Choosing rr_tolerance=0 is useful when checking whether the reduction relies on numerical acceptance rather than a tolerance-matched coefficient.

The original input angles must not be silently replaced by rounded source literals. Python's Qiskit-object path may already contain binary floating-point angles, while supported native Rust QASM literals can preserve their textual decimal provenance. Therefore equal-looking numerical results do not necessarily certify identical original sources.

items.title: Reduction-only and hybrid
items.text:
• method="reduction_rules" returns a classification when reduction establishes one; otherwise it can report unknown.
  • method="hybrid" passes the final configured reduction residual to WMC only when reduction remains inconclusive. It does not revert to the original unreduced circuit behind the user's back.
  • method="wmc_only" bypasses reduction-rule matching but still performs the representation/normalization required to form the WMC problem.

An accepted reduction can depend on rr_tolerance. When a source-exact or independently certified claim matters, compare with an appropriate mathematical oracle or use controlled exact-source checks.

See worked examples, weighted model counting, and equivalence and numerical semantics.

items.title: Python API
items.text:
The primary supported Python import is:

from QuPRS import check_equivalence

The generated signatures below come from the Python source tree. Only explicitly selected API entry points are documented; Python implementation helpers and private Rust worker modules are not part of this API reference.

items.title: check_equivalence(circuit1, circuit2, method='hybrid', strategy='Difference', tool_name='gpmc', timeout=600, safe_mode=False, backend='python', wmc_phase_tolerance=None, approximate_distance_tolerance=1e-08, rr_tolerance=None, phase_tolerance=None, gpmc_precision_digits=30)
items.text:
Check whether two quantum circuits are equivalent using different verification methods.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default circuit1 str | QuantumCircuit

The first quantum circuit to compare. It can be a file path or a Qiskit circuit object.

required circuit2 str | QuantumCircuit

The second quantum circuit to compare. It can be a file path or a Qiskit circuit object.

required method str

Verification method. Default is "hybrid". - 'hybrid': Uses both Reduction Rules (RR) and Weighted Model Counting (WMC). This is the recommended mode. - 'reduction_rules': Uses only Reduction Rules. If reduction is incomplete, returns 'unknown'. - 'wmc_only': Uses Weighted Model Counting (WMC), without reduction-rule matching. Python still normalizes phase coefficients while building the PathSum, but preserves small nonzero input phases rather than removing them using the local reduction tolerance.

'hybrid' strategy str

Internal strategy for handling quantum gates. Default is "Difference". - 'Difference': Uses a difference-based strategy. - 'Proportional': Uses a proportional strategy. - 'Naive': Uses a naive strategy. - 'Straightforward': Uses a straightforward strategy.

'Difference' timeout int

Requested deadline in seconds (default 600). The external WMC subprocess consumes only the remaining monotonic budget. In-process Rust and Python symbolic work on a non-main thread are NOT subject to a strict end-to-end hard timeout. Rust safe_mode=True supervises a separate worker with a monotonic deadline; parent-side Qiskit serialization remains non-preemptible. Solver/process/parse failures do not imply circuit inequivalence.

600 safe_mode bool

For the Python backend, use the existing strategy isolation; for the Rust backend, invoke PyO3 inside an isolated child worker with bounded IPC and a supervised deadline. Worker isolation alone does not guarantee a physical-memory cap or cleanup of solver processes that detach from its process group. Default is False.

False rr_tolerance float | None

Per-call RR numerical coefficient matching. Defaults to 1e-10. Preserves small source phase terms.

None phase_tolerance float | None

Phase zero classification in radians for RR and WMC; conflicts with a different wmc_phase_tolerance.

None wmc_phase_tolerance float | None

WMC phase threshold separating "equivalent" and "equivalent*" for near-unit magnitudes. None uses config.WMC_PHASE_TOLERANCE.

None approximate_distance_tolerance float | None

Projective Hilbert-Schmidt distance threshold in (0, 1), default 1e-8. None means the same default, not the removed magnitude classifier. Finite counts use one central printed-count distance verdict; raw printed uncertainty remains separately diagnostic.

1e-08 gpmc_precision_digits int

GPMC complex MPFR output/working digits: 30 by default or explicitly 90. Independent from distance tolerance.

30

Returns:

Name Type Description EquivalenceCheckResult

An object containing the result dictionary and the final PathSum circuit object.

items.title: Numerical results
items.text:
The equivalent field can report equivalent, equivalent*, not_equivalent, unknown, Timeout, or MemoryOut. An inconclusive or resource-limited result is not a proof of circuit inequivalence.

rr_tolerance, wmc_phase_tolerance (or its phase_tolerance alias), and approximate_distance_tolerance control distinct parts of verification. See Verification and the equivalence semantics.

items.title: Theory
items.text: QuPRS verifies supported unitary quantum-circuit comparisons using Boolean Path-sum representations, algebraic reduction rules, and optional complex weighted model counting.

items.title: Mathematical foundations
items.text:
• Path-sum and reduction rules explains Boolean path variables, phase-polynomial expressions, the roles of Elim/HH/omega, and exact-versus-tolerance-aware reduction.
  • Weighted model counting explains the complex counting formulation, independent solver selection, and limits of numerical evidence.
  • Verification methods and result meanings relates the mathematical stages to the user-facing API.

For two unitary operators U and V on n qubits, the projective metric used by the default WMC classifier is

\[ D_{\mathrm{proj}}(U,V) =\sqrt{1-\frac{|\operatorname{Tr}(U^\dagger V)|^2}{4^n}}. \]

An equality claim may be structural or approximate, depending on the selected method and tolerances. This distance is global-phase invariant, but a positive finite-precision solver verdict is not, by itself, a proof of source-exact equivalence.

The complete publicly documented equivalence semantics distinguish exact equality, global-phase equivalence, and finite numerical acceptance. See executable examples for small controls.

items.title: Verification methods and results
items.text:
The public Python QuPRS.check_equivalence() interface supports three methods.

Method What runs When it can be inconclusive hybrid Path-sum reduction, then WMC on the final residual when reduction is inconclusive A solver failure or resource limit is not a negative proof reduction_rules Reduction rules without an external WMC solver An irreducible or unsupported symbolic residual may yield unknown wmc_only WMC path without reduction-rule matching Finite solver arithmetic and unsupported inputs can limit reliability

Use tool_name="gpmc" or tool_name="ganak" for an explicit WMC backend. No implicit fallback changes the chosen solver.

items.title: Result meanings
items.text:
Status Interpretation equivalent An accepted exact or tolerance-dependent identity under the selected method equivalent* An accepted result up to global phase, distinct from exact matrix equality not_equivalent A supported symbolic counterexample or numerical WMC rejection unknown No conclusive answer from the selected path Timeout / MemoryOut A resource-limited run, not non-equivalence Exception Invalid input, unsupported operations or failed solver/parse, not non-equivalence

Check wmc_solver_invoked instead of assuming that a non-null wmc_time means an external solver ran. Numerical classifications may contain separately reported precision diagnostics; their presence does not amount to certified solver error bounds.

items.title: Independent tolerances
items.text:
• rr_tolerance defaults to 1e-10 and influences reduction coefficient matching.
  • phase_tolerance (alias wmc_phase_tolerance) distinguishes a negligible global phase, in radians.
  • approximate_distance_tolerance defaults to 1e-8 and applies to the projective Hilbert–Schmidt distance.
  • gpmc_precision_digits is 30 by default; an explicit value of 90 is supported for GPMC, not Ganak.

Do not confuse a projective distance threshold with an angular tolerance or solver decimal output precision.

items.title: Input and execution boundaries
items.text:
QuPRS verifies unitary circuit behavior, not measurement outcomes, reset channels or open-system semantics. QASM versions and gate sets have documented, backend-dependent limits.

backend="python" selects the Python implementation; backend="rust" uses PyO3. With the Rust backend, safe_mode=True supervises a child process that invokes the same Rust extension. It is not a call to the standalone CLI, and parent-side serialization remains outside the worker's hard deadline.

See the executable examples, Path-sum theory, WMC contract, architecture, and Python API.

items.title: Weighted model counting and solver contracts
From a residual Path-sum to weighted counting
items.text:
When reduction cannot complete a comparison, QuPRS can encode the remaining symbolic expression into a weighted Boolean formula. A generic weighted model count is

\[ \operatorname{WMC}(F)= \sum_{\sigma\models F}\;\prod_{\ell\in\sigma}w(\ell), \]

where \(F\) is a Boolean formula, \(\sigma\) ranges over satisfying assignments, and the literal weights \(w\) may be complex. The circuit-specific encoding and trace normalization determine how the count contributes to the comparison; the generic formula alone is not a full circuit verification algorithm.

The default numerical equivalence metric is the projective Hilbert–Schmidt distance:

\[ D_{\mathrm{proj}}(U,V)= \sqrt{1-\frac{|\operatorname{Tr}(U^\dagger V)|^2}{4^n}}, \]

for two unitary operators on n qubits. It is unchanged by a global phase. The default approximate_distance_tolerance=1e-8 applies to this distance, not to a raw trace-magnitude defect or an angle in radians.

Writing \(d=2^n\) and \(m=|\operatorname{Tr}(U^\dagger V)|/d\), exact global-phase equivalence requires \(m=1\). The two commonly used distances are distinct:

\[ \begin{aligned} D_{\mathrm{proj}}^2 &= 1-m^2,\\ D_{\mathrm{gp}}^2 &= 2-2m,\\ D_{\mathrm{proj}}^2 &= D_{\mathrm{gp}}^2-\frac{D_{\mathrm{gp}}^4}{4}. \end{aligned} \]

For the single-qubit Qiskit rotation \(R_z(\theta)\), the analytic control is

\[ D_{\mathrm{proj}}(I,R_z(\theta))= |\sin(\theta/2)|. \]

These are mathematical properties of unitary matrices, not certificates of external solver arithmetic. The actual WMC stage uses a finite-precision complex count; source semantics, numeric verdicts, and printed-count resolution remain separate.

items.title: Supported external solvers
items.text:
User selection Weight format Numerical characteristics tool_name="gpmc" Paired complex real/imaginary weights Default 30 decimal working/output digits; 90 may be explicitly requested using gpmc_precision_digits=90 tool_name="ganak" Signed complex weights Native printed precision; may be too coarse for some tight distance thresholds

Solver selection is explicit, and unsupported choices, missing executables, malformed or nonfinite results, and failed processes must not silently fall back to a different solver. The exact invocation and count parser depend on the backend.

The phase classification threshold phase_tolerance (or wmc_phase_tolerance) is in radians, while rr_tolerance governs reduction coefficient matching. The three user-facing tolerances—reduction matching, global-phase classification, and projective-distance acceptance—serve different purposes and are independently configurable. gpmc_precision_digits is a separate numerical solver setting; there is no supported process-global mutable WMC policy.

items.title: Understanding the returned evidence
items.text:
The following Python result fields have distinct meanings:

Field Interpretation equivalent Operational status: equivalent, equivalent*, not_equivalent, unknown, Timeout, MemoryOut wmc_time WMC stage timing, if that stage was reached wmc_solver_invoked Whether an external weighted counter actually ran wmc_numerical_verdict Solver-derived numerical classification where available wmc_print_resolution_distance Printed-output granularity diagnostic, not an internal solver-error certificate rr_approximate Whether an accepted reduction was tolerance-dependent where reported

A weighted formula admitting an exact unweighted tautology shortcut can be counted analytically without launching a solver. For that reason, wmc_time alone is not proof that GPMC or Ganak ran.

Caution: finite-precision complex counts do not generally certify source-exact operator equality. A near-threshold observation may require an independent unitary oracle, algebraic proof, or tighter evidence. An execution error, unknown or resource limit is not a proof of inequality.

See executable examples, Path-sum rules, Python API, and the published numerical evidence description.
